newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canada and U.S. firms cooperate on PCS services.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canada and U.S. firms cooperate on PCS services.

text.p: A Canadian telecommunications company signed a cooperation agreement on Wednesday with three big U.S. companies to share their new wireless telephone networks known as personal communications services (PCS).

Montreal-based Microcell Telecommunications Inc signed a roaming agreement with Pacific Bell Mobile Services, of Pleasonton, Ca., BellSouth Mobility DCS, of Atlanta, Ga., and Omnipoint Corp, of Arlington, Va. Pacific Bell is a unit of Pacific Telesis Group.
Under the accord, subscribers of any one company will be able to use their wireless telephones in territories licensed to the other companies.

Montreal customers, for example, would be able to use their PCS handsets in New York City, while those from New York's Westchester County will able to keep in contact with their head office while in Montreal.

PCS is seen as the next generation of wireless telecommunications technology and a direct competitor of cellular telephone networks. PCS providers are investing an estimated $5 billion to build their North American networks.

Microcell, a private company owned by several Canadian telecommunications concerns, including Groupe Videotron Ltee, of Montreal and Shaw Communications Inc, of Calgary, is one of two holders of a national Canadian PCS license.

Pacific Bell holds PCS operating licenses for California and Nevada, while Omnipoint covers many northeastern U.S. states and parts of others such as Arkansas, Texas and Oklahoma. BellSouth Mobility's network includes North and South Carolina and eastern Tennessee.

The roaming agreement came two days ahead of Microcell's launch of Fido, Canada's first PCS network. Microcell said it planned to offer PCS coverage in the greater Montreal area on Friday. A Canadian rollout will follow, with Quebec City, Ottawa, Toronto and Vancouver being added by mid-1997.
Microcell President Andre Tremblay told a press conference that subscribers of the Canadian company will be able to use their Fido handsets in the New York area by the first quarter of 1997.
"You can expect to see a very quick ramp up on those agreements," Tremblay said.

Lyndon Daniels, president and chief executive of Pacific Bell Mobile, said the roaming pact is historic because it adds Canada to the list of about 100 countries worldwide using a standard for wireless communications systems called Global Systems for Mobile Communications (GSM).
"This is the first North American roaming agreement that goes outside the United States," Daniels said.

GSM is fully digital and is based on an Integrated Services Digital Network that network operators claim offers numerous advantages over analog cellular telephone networks. Calls made to and from PCS mobile telephones using GSM standards are protected against eavesdropping because they are encrypted, and the digital handsets use less battery power.
The executives said more such PCS roaming agreements were expected in the next year covering all of North America.
